02.caption: Where we land first: of 8,445 insured US institutions, 262 sit in the 5-to-150-billion band, big enough to carry the full regulatory load and small enough to buy rather than build.
Above 150 billion there are about 20 banks, and they build in-house; below 5 billion, a bank cannot carry the load at all.
Our worked example is Larkspur Bank, 18 billion and fictional: 1.1 million customers, a 420-seat contact center, 50,000 emails a month, all replaced by the customer's own mail in week one.

03.caption: An email is a written error notice under Reg E, so the clock starts the moment it lands: 10 business days to act, 45 days to resolve, and 90 for POS, foreign or first-30-day cases.
A half-sentence inside a friendly email still counts as notice, so an unread inbox is a liability, not a queue.
Email is also the slowest and priciest channel the bank runs: 6 to 12 dollars a contact, 27 hours to a first reply, 22 percent of threads ending in "please call us".
And 28 percent of agent time goes to switching systems and re-typing, not to the customer.

04.caption: Scope comes from one sort: volume, determinability and whether identity can be achieved, all gated by penalty risk. One line follows: everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person.
Phase 1 takes general inquiries, account servicing, transactions and dispute intake, which is 80 percent of the volume. Payments and payoff wait for phase 2.
Complaints, fraud and off-brief mail are human-only from day one: detected, clocked and handed to a person. Spam is archived before intake ever sees it.

05.caption: Every email runs the same five steps: ingest with an arrival timestamp, sort into a category and an identity level, decide on the matrix, resolve, then verify for 14 days.
The matrix picks the road per category: general inquiries run auto, servicing runs at one click or above, transactions can also be human-signed, and complaints and fraud have no road at all.
Only step 4 ever reaches the customer, and it does not write. It assembles a compliance-locked template, account-data slots, and the connective tissue, one line in five.

06.caption: Every cell is a product of two: the category sets the row, the identity level of the sender sets the column, and R times I gives L, where the human sits.
Where identity is missing, servicing and transactions are locked: the reply is a locked template that carries no account data, and step-up opens the rest.
Complaints have no road on email at all, because the tool functions do not exist on this channel, and disputes stay L1, human-signed, permanently.
Nothing starts autonomous: backtest, shadow, then dual sign-off by compliance and operations, with auto-demotion on drift. Graduation never unlocks a locked cell.

07.caption: This is the user experience to judge: risk and identity decide who acts, AI or human, on every email.
Demo 1 plays here: identity assurance. A customer verifies inside the thread, and the AI is disclosed there.
The other demos live on YouTube, and the running prototype is one click away from this page.

08.caption: Onboarding runs on the bank's own material: 90 days of historical email, and the policy and process playbook it already works from.

Our tools compile it: category discovery proposes the bank's category set for an admin to confirm, and the policy compiler turns the playbook into the bank's own R times I matrix, carrying its thresholds, approval nodes and clocks.
The connectors come prebuilt: mailbox, core banking, CRM, identity and the archive, so the bank's systems stay where they are.
The bank signs the result before anything runs, on the same path as the pilot: backtest, shadow, dual sign-off. One runtime, per-bank configuration, so the next bank takes weeks.

09.caption: The headline is the verified autonomous resolution rate: 25 to 35 percent by six months, where resolved means no human touch and no reopen within 14 days, and the number has to survive QA sampling.

Time to resolution, not to first reply, measured from the arrival timestamp: under 15 minutes when it runs autonomously, under a day otherwise, disputes excepted, against a 3.2-day baseline that is still an assumption.

And a veto stands over it: one critical error voids the whole rate. A key error is a wrong action, a wrong party, a missed clock or a broken promise, so the bar is zero key errors, clocks at 100 percent, and recall of at least 99.5 percent. Non-negotiable.
Twelve guardrails run alongside, and the 35 percent ROI base case is the top of this band, at steady state.
